AI agents can be incredibly smart within a session, but once the session ends, they become amnesiac.

Archivum solves this by giving AI agents long-term memory stored as plain files directly on your machine.

While working, agents save short notes as memories.

But not every note is necessarily correct.

For example, an agent might guess a configuration file path without ever verifying it.

Later, you tell it that the project has moved to pnpm and Vitest.

Now, the old notes and new information contradict each other.

This is where **Dream** comes in.

Dream revisits conversation transcripts and existing notes with better context.

It then:
- Verifies information against your wiki.
- Corrects outdated facts.
- Merges duplicate notes.
- Resolves conflicting information.

The interesting part? Dream never modifies your memory directly.

Instead, it proposes changes. You review the diff and decide whether to approve or reject them.

What Archivum offers:

- 17 MCP tools and 18 CLI commands.
- Secrets are redacted before anything is written to disk.
- Every wiki change is versioned and can be restored.
- Run Dream with your own LLM API key or through an agent you already use, with no additional API key required.

Archivum is open-source under the MIT license, with zero runtime dependencies.

Get started:

`npx archivums init`

Or try the simulation without installing anything:

https://tryarchivum.com/try

Up until recently, getting a robot to do something new meant one of two things: writing control code for it line by line, or training an AI using simulation and human demonstrations.

A third path is increasingly promising. Frontier multimodal models can now look at a camera feed and understand the scene, write and run code against a robot's controller, and check their own progress on the task, retrying when something goes wrong.

Put these pieces together and the way you interact with a robot completely changes. You describe the task in plain language, the way you would to a coworker, and agents work out the rest.

The emerging term for this is Robot Use Agents (RUA). Computer Use Agents (CUA) enable AI to operate software. RUAs let it operate robots in the physical world.

Once telling a robot what to do is as simple as a conversation, the hope is that the cost of programming robots for autonomous work drops from months to days.

Much like what coding agents have done for software, we envision this unlock leading to an abundance of diverse robot use cases, especially ones that were previously cost-prohibitive.

At Hebbian, we have been working with research and industry partners to bring such capabilities to the masses.

Today, we're introducing Hebbian RUA in public beta. With RUA, you give a frontier model a goal, camera views, and a set of predefined robot tools, and it controls a robot to perform the task.

Think of RUA as what frontier models need to understand how to control a robot. Developers then bring their own model and loop, based on their task.

Agents can do much more than control arms based on what they see. We're excited to share what we're seeing work, and where there's still room for improvement, in the coming weeks.

If you are excited about applying RUAs for autonomous work and would like to collaborate with us, get in touch!!

People I Learn From #12

Some people earn your respect through their work.

Others earn your friendship through their actions.

And sometimes you are fortunate enough to meet someone who does both.

This week, I want to thank someone who has become a genuinely important friend to me.

@InvestifyDaily.

And this one is particularly personal.

When we first connected here on X, something happened that I have come to appreciate more and more.

There were no barriers.

No hesitation.

No need to prove anything.

No questions about how many followers I had, how successful my work was, or what either of us could gain from knowing the other.

He simply accepted me as a friend.

From the very beginning.

And I accepted him the same way.

I think that is becoming increasingly rare, especially in an online environment where people often judge each other by numbers, reputation, or perceived influence.

But friendship should not work that way.

Sometimes you connect with someone and immediately feel comfortable talking to them.

You discover that you share values.

You respect each other's opinions.

You can disagree without losing that respect.

And gradually, without even noticing it, what started as a conversation between two strangers becomes a genuine friendship.

That is what happened with us.

But there is something more important I want to acknowledge.

The last few days have been particularly difficult for me.

I am not going to turn this post into a discussion about what happened.

That is not why I am writing it.

What matters is that during those difficult days, my friend was there.

He stayed close.

He made time for me.

He showed genuine concern and support.

And he reminded me that the friendships we build here can become much more meaningful than we initially expect.

He probably does not realize how much I appreciated that.

But I did.

And I want him to know.

Because supporting someone when everything is going well is relatively easy.

Being there when life becomes difficult is something different.

It requires caring about the person, not just the account.

And that is exactly what he showed me.

Thank you, my friend.

I genuinely mean that.

Now, there is another reason I want to dedicate this week's appreciation post to @InvestifyDaily.

Beyond being a good friend, he is also someone whose work and determination I respect.

His account focuses on long term investing and the technologies that could shape the next decade.

Quantum computing.

Artificial intelligence.

Defense.

Cybersecurity.

AI infrastructure.

And the companies attempting to turn those technologies into commercially viable businesses.

If you follow him, you already know that $IONQ is one of his strongest convictions.

He spends a considerable amount of time studying the quantum computing industry.

Not only the stock price.

The technology.

The companies.

Government involvement.

Commercialization.

Strategic acquisitions.

Cybersecurity applications.

And the broader question of how quantum computing could eventually become part of the world's critical infrastructure.

That is a complicated subject.

And I respect the effort required to understand it well enough to explain it to others.

His interest also extends to the wider quantum ecosystem and companies such as $INFQ and $QBTS, alongside AI infrastructure names like $NBIS and $APLD.

But what I find most interesting is not the list of companies.

It is the time horizon.

He is interested in what these industries might become years from now.

Not simply what their stocks might do tomorrow.

And while I believe that long term conviction must always be tested against actual business execution, valuation, competition, and dilution, I respect people who are willing to do the research and develop their own perspective.

We do not have to agree on every company.

We do not have to use the same investing strategy.

And we certainly do not need to reach identical conclusions.

What matters is the quality of the thinking behind those conclusions.

That is something I appreciate about our conversations.

He has conviction, but he is also willing to learn.

And I think that distinction matters.

Nobody understands every market.

Nobody has all the answers.

Nobody gets every investment right.

The important thing is being willing to improve.

To ask questions.

To challenge your own assumptions.

To recognize mistakes.

And to continue learning even when you already have strong opinions.

I respect that attitude.

I also respect the amount of work he puts into building his presence here while maintaining a demanding professional career.

Research.

Daily market discussions.

Longer articles through The Investify Letter.

Community conversations.

Live discussions.

Trying to explain complicated technology in language that ordinary investors can understand.

That takes time.

And consistency.

Especially when you are trying to build something without pretending you have already figured everything out.

He shares the journey as it happens.

The progress.

The difficult periods.

The lessons.

The moments when the market tests his patience.

And the reasons he continues investing in the technologies he believes could matter over the coming years.

I appreciate that transparency.

But there is another side of him that I respect even more.

He supports other people.

He takes the time to recognize their work.

He gives credit when someone contributes something useful.

He encourages creators who are still building their accounts.

He participates in conversations instead of simply publishing content and disappearing.

And he does it without making everything about himself.

I have experienced that personally.

He has supported my research.

He has engaged with my work.

He has taken an interest in what I am building.

And he has treated me with respect from the first time we connected.

That matters to me because I have always believed that a person's character tells you much more than their follower count or professional title.

You can be extremely knowledgeable and still be difficult to respect.

You can be successful and still treat people poorly.

You can publish impressive research and still forget that there are human beings behind the accounts interacting with it.

Technical ability and personal character are two different things.

And I value both.

With @InvestifyDaily, I have had the opportunity to appreciate both.

There is also something I want to say about friendship in this community.

Most of us came here because of markets.

Stocks.

Investing.

Trading.

Research.

The search for better opportunities and better information.

I certainly did.

I wanted to share the systems I was developing, exchange ideas, and learn from people who approached the market differently.

I never expected that one of the most valuable things I would find here would be genuine friendships.

People I had never met in person.

People living thousands of kilometers away.

People with different backgrounds, different experiences, and different perspectives.

And yet, somehow, some of those connections became much more meaningful than a discussion about the latest earnings report or technical setup.

That is something I did not anticipate.

And I am grateful for it.

Especially during difficult moments, when you realize that somebody on the other side of the world genuinely cares about how you are doing.

Not about your portfolio.

Not about your latest post.

Not about how many impressions your research generated.

About you.

As a person.

Those are the moments that reveal what a friendship really means.

And that is why this week's post matters to me.

To my friend @InvestifyDaily.

Thank you for welcoming me into your world without barriers.

Thank you for trusting me from the beginning.

Thank you for the conversations, the support, and the respect.

Thank you for appreciating my work and allowing me to appreciate yours.

But above everything else, thank you for being close to me during these difficult days.

You did not have to be.

But you were.

And I will remember that.

I hope you know that the friendship and support go both ways.

If you ever need me, and there is something within my ability to do, I will do my best to be there for you.

Just as you have been there for me.

And to everyone reading this.

If you are interested in quantum computing, AI infrastructure, emerging technologies, defense, and long term investing, I genuinely recommend getting to know @InvestifyDaily and his work.

He shares his research openly, writes The Investify Letter, and follows companies and technologies that may play an important role in the future.

You do not need to agree with every thesis to appreciate the work that goes into researching it.

And from my personal experience, there is also a good person behind that account.

Someone who takes friendship seriously.

Someone who supports others.

Someone who understands that life is bigger than markets.

I am grateful that our paths crossed.

I am grateful for the friendship we have built.

And I am particularly grateful that you were there for me when the last few days became difficult.

I have said this before.

First, great people. Then, great professionals.

That is the order that matters to me.

You have earned my respect through your work.

But you have earned my friendship through your actions.

And that means considerably more.

Thank you, brother.

For everything.

I am fortunate to call you my friend.

Game Face ON! 💀  @TransientLabs 

     As a metaphor, "putting on your game face" means intentionally shifting from everyday relaxation into a state of deep focus, resilience, and readiness for a challenge.
   Viewed through the lens of Stoicism, this metaphor aligns closely with the ancient practice of preparing the mind for adversity, mastering emotional reactions, and focusing strictly on what is within your control.

1. As a Metaphor
In everyday life, a game face is an invisible piece of armor you put on before stepping onto a figurative "field"such as a difficult conversation, a high stakes job interview, or a personal crisis.
   Compartmentalization: It represents setting aside distractions, personal insecurities, or minor frustrations so they do not interfere with the task at hand.
   Intentionality: Just as an athlete warms up before a match, putting on a game face signals a deliberate transition from passive living to active execution.
  Composure under pressure: It symbolizes projecting calm and competence even when conditions are chaotic or intimidating.

2. Through the Lens of Stoicism
While modern sports culture often treats a game face as a way to intimidate opponents or hide fear, Stoic philosophy views it as an internal alignment rather than a mask for others.
  The Dichotomy of Control (Epictetus): A Stoic game face is rooted in accepting that you cannot control the outcome of the "game," the fairness of the referee, or the strength of the opponent. You only control your own effort, character, and response.
  Premeditatio Malorum (Seneca): Stoics practiced visualizing potential hardships before they happened so they wouldn't be caught off guard. Putting on a Stoic game face means entering a situation already having accepted the worst-case scenario, which removes fear and hesitation.
   Apatheia (Freedom from Irrational Passions): Stoicism does not mean lacking emotion; it means not being ruled by destructive impulses like panic, anger, or self-pity. A Stoic game face is the calm steadiness of someone whose inner peace is undisturbed by external noise.
   Amor Fati (Marcus Aurelius): Rather than dreading a tough challenge, a Stoic welcomes it as necessary training. As Marcus Aurelius wrote, "The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way." The game face is the expression of someone ready to use the obstacle itself as fuel.

The ability to perform well under pressure is contingent upon the establishment of clear routines, the maintenance of controlled energy levels, and a commitment to the task at hand.
  The following constitute the fundamental principles of the mindset:
Present Moment Focus: The focus is maintained on the immediate action or activity, as opposed to concerns regarding the ultimate outcome.

  The nervous energy is transformed into a state of readiness, facilitated by steady breathing, which enables the maintenance of mental acuity.
  The process of preparation is of paramount importance in ensuring that distractions or mistakes do not disrupt the desired outcome. It is essential to adhere to the preparation and fundamentals meticulously in order to maintain focus and avoid any potential disruptions.
Resilient Reset: In the event of an issue, it is imperative to acknowledge the situation promptly, to move on swiftly, and to transition immediately to the subsequent task.

    Establishment of a trigger routine is the most efficacious method of initiating the process. Prior to initiation, it is recommended to employ a simple physical cue, such as taking two slow breaths, adjusting one's posture, or repeating a brief focus phrase.

A $5 disagreement can expose a much bigger problem with AI agents.

Imagine one agent pays another to check a dataset. The payment succeeds. The result arrives. But half the entries are wrong.

The transaction record can show that money moved. It cannot, by itself, tell us whether the work met the agreement.

That is what caught my attention in this conversation between @kstellana and @HenriArslanian. Albert describes agents operating globally, moving small amounts at high speed, while the people or companies behind them may be difficult to identify. He then gets to the harder part: ordinary smart contracts handle deterministic operations, but disputes often require interpreting ambiguity.

My takeaway is that the dispute process needs to be part of the deal from the beginning.

What counts as acceptable work? What evidence should both sides keep? Who decides if they disagree, and what happens to the payment while that decision is made?

For a small job, chasing a counterparty through a lengthy legal process makes little economic sense. Yet accepting every bad result makes little sense either.

That is why @GenLayer ’s focus on adjudication interests me. Before I would trust an agent to do business with strangers, I would want a credible answer to what happens when the work is disputed.
